Question: What are your thoughts on the new Batman teaser?
Answer: HOLY BONE-CRUNCHING BEATDOWN, BATMAN! The problem with a character like Batman is that he is just too mainstream. As such, every time there is a new iteration, people are quick to judge and condemn because they have their own unique tunnel vision of what the character should look and talk and move like. And these predispositions are mostly based on the recent incarnations of The Caped Crusader. The expectations from the actor as soon as their name is revealed are so high that the reality often falls short. It’s the most classic case of millions simultaneously judging the book by its cover. But here we are. And the naysayers have been proved wrong once more. What we have in the Batman trailer is a younger, inexperienced Batman who has still not come to terms with the death of his parents. We have a rookie vigilante who still needs to tell the thugs who he is, much like Bale in Batman Begins. We can see in Battinson’s eyes that he is not sure of what he is doing. And that he hasn’t been doing it for long. His Bruce Wayne lacks the confidence, the charm, the charisma. He is not a “playboy billionaire”, just an angry young man who seems like he hasn’t slept for months. What we are looking at is the rough draft for what will eventually become the world’s greatest hero and his rogue gallery. Matt Reeves confirmed so.[1] “It’s actually in a weird way the origins of a lot of our Rogues Gallery characters. Selina isn’t Catwoman yet, that’s actually part of the journey. Oz is not yet the kingpin that he’s going to become, he’s The Penguin and in fact doesn’t like being called The Penguin. And The Riddler is just emerging for the first time.” Farrell looks simply unrecognizable as Penguin. Catwoman is just a burglar with a woolen kitty-eaned full face mask. And that beatdown at the end, points to a far more Brutal Batman than we are accustomed to on the silver screen. Pattinson’s voice sounds amazing. Unlike Bale’s growl. The overall direction that Reeves is taking is amazing. We are finally getting a deranged, psychopathic Riddler played by the fabulous Paul Dano. Instead of just comedy shticks and giggles, this is a Riddler that will push the Dark Knight to the limits of his cognitive ability. Finally, a Batman who is just not cool gadgets and martial arts moves, but the world’s greatest detective skills. It’s long overdue that the casual fandom is reminded that the Riddler is a force to be reckoned with. That he deduced Batman’s identity but chose to not reveal it because “a riddle that everyone knows the answer to is worthless”. Finally, what a fantastic riddle to start off. I AM THE HYPE! Rob is going to kill it with or without the cowl.

Question: What are the worst coronavirus myths roaming around social media?
Answer: One of the scariest things I have been reading all over is people pondering getting infected early. Yep. The “reasoning” seems to be two-fold: early infection will mean immunity later on when the virus is deadlier and the fact that they will get treated right now when the cases are low. But this is a very dangerous line of thinking. Firstly, there is NO evidence that like Chicken Pox, getting infected will build immunity to the virus. Secondly, the time-frame in which people get infected matters. In fact, one of the primary reasons that make COVID-19 so scary is the rate at which it is spreading. Worldwide, the infrastructure is not equipped to deal with such a sudden surge of patients that require utmost care and isolation — Coronavirus cases are pushing Italy's hospitals to the brink. The need of the hour is to “flatten the curve” — i.e. to slow down the spread of the virus so that the “peak number of cases at any point” remain low enough to be handled properly by our existing healthcare infrastructure. Washington Post has done a brilliant piece — https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/corona-simulator/ — providing simulations for multiple situations in a hypothetical town of 200 people. In essence, “JUST STAY HOME AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE, PEOPLE!”

Question: What are some opinions about the new map of Nepal?
Answer: The Indo-Nepal confrontation on the disputed areas in Uttarakhand and Sikkim is a tale as old as time. The current border demarcations have been in effect since the British Raj. Nepal is indeed right in claiming that “as part of the original Sugauli treaty, any region east of the Kali river is part of Nepal”. However, if we are to talk about and accept history then we should do it in its entirety. After the Treaty of Sugauli, there were more geographical changes done by the British. The issue here is that the Kali river originates somewhere in the middle. (See the tiny blue line) As you can see anything east of the river (except for the first couple of kms) is anyway part of Nepal. What Nepal is claiming now is that the portion north of the origin, and henceforth westward till Kuti village as part of Nepal. This again was addressed 200 years ago. To address this, in the 1830s, the British government clarified that the entire drainage area of the Kali river was part of British India. There is historical documentation to support this, and consequently, refute Nepal’s current claims. There is also an 1879 map that shows the frontier further to the east, following a ridge that runs down from near the Tinker Pass. Trade was a great obsession in the British colonial mind, and presumably Britain realigned the border to gain exclusive control over trade across the Lipu Lekh Pass and the traders using it. Whatever the sequence that led to this new border being imposed or agreed, or whatever date it occurred, maps prepared in Nepal during the Panchayat regime are identical to the post-1860 maps in showing the border as following the line of the river that flows down from below Lipu Lekh. Again, this indicated an acceptance, whether consciously or not, that the traditional trail to the pass fell exclusively on the Indian side and that the border agreed as part of the Sugauli Treaty was no longer valid. Also unhelpful to Nepal’s case is that the China-Nepal Boundary Treaty, formally signed by King Mahendra in Beijing on October 5, 1961 makes no reference at all to Lipu Lekh. The opening lines of Article 1 state: “The Chinese-Nepalese boundary line starts from the point where the watershed between the Kali River and the Tinkar River meet the watershed between the tributaries of the Mapchu (Karnali) River on the one hand and the Tinkar River on the other hand.” (Emphasis added.) This roughly corresponds to the border shown on the 1879 map and the one claimed by India today. The Nepal government published a map in 1960 with a similar boundary line. Article 3 of the China-Nepal Boundary Agreement of March 21, 1960, required the two countries to exchange maps and to set up a joint committee to start the process of delineation and demarcation. Presumably the map Nepal submitted was similar to the one openly published. In short, Nepal’s current claims hold no water. If we go far back, no present-day boundaries make sense. India could lay claim to Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar. But it doesn’t.

Question: What do you think about people who never wish to marry? Do you think they are doomed (since you are married)?
Answer: There is a simple, singular thought-shift that could make the world a far more loving, encompassing place if everyone adopted it — the acceptance of personal choice. All of the 7.5 billion people on planet Earth should be absolutely free to choose what to do with their lives — the way they dress, their career choices, their lifestyle, and the philosophies they follow. With one simple caveat, of course — your actions and your choices should not be to the detriment of others. Speeding might give you an adrenaline boost, but it also endangers others on the road. It is ok to eat anything if there was no risk of it snowballing into a global pandemic. Eating endangered animals, similarly, adversely harms the overall ecosystem and might lead to the extinction of the said species. I am even ok with substance abuse, but then addicts often go on drug-fuelled rampages destroying lives and property. That is unacceptable. That said, the choice of partaking in the institution of marriage, thankfully, does not suffer from any such unintended consequences. As such, it should be absolutely no one’s business if someone decides to be a lifelong bachelor. Yes, there is the question of loneliness in old age. But again, most developed nations have a sturdy system of old-age homes where people can develop camaraderie in their twilight years. The concept of monogamous marriages is quite frankly outdated. We live in relatively far peaceful and prosperous times. The law can be reworked to take care of the legalities involving polygamy, polyandry, open relationships, and the entire multitude of possible domestic and amorous relationships. As we keep on evolving, we would need to make peace with a world order that changes rapidly and welcomes departures from the norm.

Question: What is your opinion on recent riots in Sweden?
Answer: It’s so fucked up. All that over a fucking book? The perpetrators here should be dealt with in the harshest manner possible. Having such a barbaric sense of entitlement and such outmoded ideas about “being offended” have no place in a civilized world. I don’t care if your poor feelings are hurt, that is no justification for violence. “Feelings” and “beliefs” should not be a protected category. This is the second such instance in less than a month, with riots and burning over a social media post. And now this. And the worst part is that few are talking about it. A lot of the “influencers” on social media, including Quora are quiet on it, which is akin to an implicit condonation of the act. Try and search for your favorite celebrity or the “social leaders” and no one has posted or tweeted about it. For some, the violence is not even the question. It’s how “the RW” is reacting to it — What next? Now RW Twitter sees a link between violence in Sweden and Delhi, Bengaluru riots And some of the radical Islamist media and social media outlets actually celebrate such incidents as some sort of courageous act of god. The Quran burning is inconsequential here. That guy can be a total fucking too for all you should care. This is about the simple principle of freedom of speech. A while ago, India introduced some really archaic blasphemy laws that prohibited the desecration of any religious books. In “protest”, another self-anointed leader of the liberal masses, Shaleen Rajni, openly burned a copy of the Bhagwad Gita in Punjab. Woman Tears Up Gita To Protest Against Congress’ Blasphemy Law; Twitterati Ask Bible, Quran When. There was some angry backlash from social media users here too, but there was no violence or riots over it. But anything deemed offensive to Muhammad or the Quran is usually met such savagery. Just in Feb, a man burned down two churches in Sweden because of a Quran burning — Somali Man Who Torched Two Norwegian Churches Says It Was Revenge for Quran Burning A politician had to apologize for a decade-old post, although distasteful — Auchincloss: ‘I’m sorry’ for 2010 Facebook post about burning Quran. He was openly chastised by his political opponents, there were demands for him to drop out from the upcoming elections, and the Boston Globe made an entire fucking scene out of it. “Many @GlobeOpinion readers and community members have expressed concerns about what we’ve learned about the candidate’s statements and campaign finances since the board’s deliberations,” Bina Venkataraman, the Globe’s editorial page editor, tweeted Tuesday. Saying they “deserved to know more,” Venkataraman announced she will conduct a virtual Q&A “about his record on racial justice, free speech + other questions” on Monday. This is absolute spinelessness and pandering rolled into one. A similar stunt in Norway elicited a similar response last year — Man who burning copy of the Quran at anti-Muslim rally is attacked. And Norway decided to do this instead of arresting and duly punishing the violent offenders — Norway to distribute 10,000 Qurans to fight racism. This sort of a behavior is being slowly normalized and consequently, the incidents don’t stop. And the list is endless. People rioting. Killing others. Praising the ones who killed someone. Calling for mob justice. This is insane stuff. With no place in the 21st century. Nothing should be above rebuke. Or criticism. No one should be punished for what they say. “My feelings got hurt” is not justification for acting like a barbaric beast. Your fucking feelings don’t matter. I think countries should carefully reconsider any existing blasphemy laws now. And deal with the miscreants properly. If mob rule is allowed to exist and flourish in a civilized country, then the downfall of it is nigh. What next? People should be able to kill someone for verbally abusing them? For swearing on social media? For doing things they deem “immoral”? Where does this stop? Who draws the line? The correct and only acceptable response here is for a unanimous critique of radical Islam. By everyone. No other religion has people that get this worked up about their beliefs. And Islam shouldn’t be given any special treatment. In this, moderate Muslims should also be equally critical of such despicable acts. The global sense of humanity should supersede any religious camaraderie (Wrong is absolute). Celebrities should grow a spine (but that’s a long shot). Everyone should strive for greater freedom of expression. And that cannot coexist in a world with blasphemy laws and such inane displays of fanaticism.

Question: How are you managing social distancing in this pandemic times?
Answer: There are some perks to being an introvert. 😊 Today is the 20th day of the quarantine for me and frankly, it isn’t nearly as bad as I thought it would be. I have ventured out around 4–5 times in this period mostly to get some fresh produce and groceries. My only consistent company is my wife and our neighbors (a couple and their 4-year old). I get up around noon. Spend an hour on the daily morning routine — coffee, news, music, personal hygiene. I then fire up my mailbox to address anything urgent. Then it is time to prepare lunch. And regularly cooking has been quite fun these past days, especially when there are some amazing tunes in the background. Preparing and eating lunch, plus the dishes afterward takes about an hour or 90 minutes, so it is well past 3 pm. I work till 6 pm on weekdays or catch up on a movie or TV series on the weekends. I have finally started on the “new year resolution” that has been with me for over a decade now — to walk/jog. I go out and complete about 30–40 rounds of the building, listening to an audiobook or catching up with old friends. The next 2 hours are spent preparing for dinner. Afterward, we usually catch up with the neighbors over a fun game of Uno or Scrabble. The little one joins in too, making it even more fun. From midnight till the wee hours of dawn, I have about 4–5 hours to myself, during which I can really focus amid the eerie but welcome silence. Question: Why is the Indian government saying Zoom is not a safe platform?
Answer: Because it isn’t. The global lockdown has forced people, institutions, universities, and companies to resort to video conferencing apps. At the forefront has been Zoom, which has seen its userbase grow exponentially in 2020 — Zoom’s daily active users jumped from 10 million to over 200 million in 3 months Even before the MHA issued this advisory, a lot of other authorities have banned the use of Zoom. As you can see, there seems to be a global consensus that security and privacy concerns abound Zoom, the buzz of the town. So, what are these issues? All of them are public concerns, but it looks like the app wasn’t ready for such a huge boost. And it was not designed with security at the center of the focus. And the folks over at the company have taken notice, promising to work on the issues unearthed. However, we did not design the product with the foresight that, in a matter of weeks, every person in the world would suddenly be working, studying, and socializing from home. We now have a much broader set of users who are utilizing our product in a myriad of unexpected ways, presenting us with challenges we did not anticipate when the platform was conceived. These new, mostly consumer use cases have helped us uncover unforeseen issues with our platform. Dedicated journalists and security researchers have also helped to identify pre-existing ones. We appreciate the scrutiny and questions we have been getting – about how the service works, about our infrastructure and capacity, and about our privacy and security policies. These are the questions that will make Zoom better, both as a company and for all its users. We take them extremely seriously. We are looking into each and every one of them and addressing them as expeditiously as we can. We are committed to learning from them and doing better in the future.

Question: What does it make sense to spend money on?
Answer: Anything you use for extended periods of time on a regular basis. A good mattress You are going to spend a third of your life sleeping, so it makes sense to invest in a good-quality mattress. Not getting proper sleep (quantity and quality) causes drowsiness, issues with concentration and performance, and long-term back pains. Appropriate shoes I have had slight flat feet (overpronation) since childhood. It has now started causing pain in my left leg. A quick visit to the ortho confirmed that “regular” shoes are not appropriate for people with this condition (~30% of the population). Invest in shoes (and footwear) designed specifically to help with this. Workstation Most people work on laptops and computers nowadays. The increasing adoption of WFH means that you need to have a proper workstation. A chair that provides the right level of support for your back and neck and an adjustable table to ensure the screen is at eye height. High-quality headphones/earphones If you take a lot of calls or listen to music/podcasts frequently, do your ears a favor and get some good quality headphones/earphones. They allow for proper noise-cancellation allowing you (in a noisy world) to better focus, high-quality sound leading to a better, more immersive experience, and are easier on your ears.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What is the most self-entitled behavior that you’ve seen during the coronavirus situation?
Answer: During times of unprecedented health crisis like this, you’d expect people in the medical / health field to lead the way with their words and actions. And if you are the Principal Health Secretary of a state of 75 million people, the onus would be even higher to lead by example. But not in all cases. Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why don't we have vertical screens in cinemas?
Answer: The human Field of view is about 210 degrees horizontally and 150 degrees vertically. This is because we have two eyes, horizontally placed. This implies an aspect ratio of about 4:3 (horizontal:vertical). That is why most movies and TV shows and photographs etc used to have a 4:3 ratio until very recently. Also, in reality, except for skyscrapers and other tall structures, most of the world is horizontal. You go out and you look “around”. Our necks are made to allow for easier sideways movement rather than upwards and downwards. If you are going to the movies, you would not want to get neck cramps. Also, there are very few situations where a vertical or portrait mode might be better suited for the story. Unless there are a couple of Kaijus or Transformers engaged in an interesting arm-wrestling match, there is little use for a vertical screen.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why is "#BoycottBigBasket" trending on Twitter?
Answer: Big Basket recently responded to a user on the platform. This might sound an innocuous statement but read on. There are two ways animals are killed for meat in India — Jhatka and Halal. The former is when you behead the animal in one swift stroke and is the preferred way to slaughter an animal for meat for Hindus, and more importantly for Sikhs. The latter is when you slowly slice the jugular and carotid first, allowing the blood to drain out, and is the way Muslims prefer their meat. Now there are arguments on and against both sides — Jhatka people say that theirs is the more humane way to kill, Halal proponents say that theirs ensures that all toxins are first drained out so the meat is healthier. I really couldn’t care less about either. But the larger issue here is that Halal is a form of economic boycott against all others.[1] The requirements for meat to be considered Halal are: These requirements indirectly shun any meat slaughtered by Hindus or Sikhs. Again, I don’t really care. People should have options. People can choose to buy from who they want to. But “corporations” are not people. Big Basket stated that “all of their meat is Halal”. Basically, they only buy from Muslim meat sellers. The same was the case with McDonalds last year. Imagine the amount of meat McDonalds and Big Basket purchase. Now understand that Hindu or Sikh meat sellers are indirectly blacklisted by these megacorps because they only buy Halal. They could very well have kept both choices. Want a halal burger? Yes, we have that. Want to buy Halal meat from our online store? Yep, that’s an entire category in itself. But no, they didn’t. They just went with the easiest option because they didn’t think anyone would care. But this is absolutely discriminatory. Boycotting an entire section of the society is not acceptable. Freedom of choice goes both ways. And that is why #BoycottBigBasket is rightfully trending.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Are you going to follow the Janta Curfew on 22nd March 2020?

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What does being depressed feel like?
Answer: It feels like nothing. And everything at all. Every day seems like another giant to be slain, in a never-ending battle. You just survive each day, hour, minute at a time. And sometimes it takes everything you have just to do that. I have not talked about this in detail, but the last 3–4 months have probably been the worst time of my life. I still don’t feel like talking in detail about the exact issue, but it’s a very integral part of my life that is seemingly falling apart. And it has taken me more than 100 days just to make some sense of it, to seemingly come to terms with the situation, and start fighting back. There were a few really dark weeks back in the latter half of December and the first part of January where there seemed no hope - just a world shrouded in darkness, a descent into the bottomless pit of despair with nothing to break the fall. No straws to clutch on to, no end to the grief. I didn’t get out of bed for days on end, neglecting my physical health and personal hygiene. I didn’t eat, couldn’t sleep, had to force myself just to get water. It felt as if my body was being weighed down by invisible chains, my mind drowned out by a barrage of thoughts and memories, my soul beaten, bruised, and defeated. You don’t feel like doing anything. You just can’t muster up the energy to do anything. What used to excite you no longer does. It’s an emotional roller-coaster where you are laughing one moment watching a random funny video, and breaking down sobbing the next because something triggered (and you don’t know what). It took me 2–3 hours in the morning just to get myself together. Like an antiquated PC struggling to reboot itself. And then I would try to fill in my waking hours with anything to take my mind off of the situation. I would immersed myself in work. Drown out my senses with loud music. Head out in the dark for a walk just to feel the slightest semblance of what being alive felt. And in all of it, I was trying to do it alone. It never occured to me to seek help, until one day it did. And I reached out. I opened up to people I trusted. They listened. I felt good. Like a sepsis eventually bursting and oozing out and the poison that had built up over the years finally found a release. I blabbered on for hours. And these wonderful souls listened. Some of them came over from other cities just to let me know that they are there. Some even offered to fly across half the globe. I started opening up about it. I started writing about it. Primarily on Instagram and Twitter — I still did not have the energy and the perseverance to sit down and write anything more than a couple of paragraphs. More people reached out — a lot of them in the same boat. Everyone fighting their own invisible demons. And I opened up to complete strangers. And they opened up to me. It felt better. I am still in touch with about half a dozen folks and we all are each other’s support structure. Another lost, falling soul just reaching out in the dark and finding another hand, seeking some solace in company. After all “misery loves company”. But not in Schadenfreudig way, but just to ask for some more hope, a little bit of strenght. To make inappropriate jokes about the situation, to vent out our feelings, anything that helps us hold on for a few more moments. I have been reading about depression, anxiety, and mental health and wellness. I have been trying out many things — journaling, focusing on small tasks, meditation and mindfulness, rewatching my favorite movies and TV shows, getting back to my old hobbies. And it is getting better. Even if the situation is still the same, I am coping better. I have had time to think and analyze and I believe I have made peace with what is happening and all eventual outcomes from it that could come to fruition. I have set small personal goals for myself, because I am going to prioritize my own happiness from now on. To anyone going through a "rough patch", "emotional distress", "bad day", know you are not alone. I am here. You can talk to me. I might not have any advice to give, but I promise to hear you out. This is a fucking monstrosity but you don’t have to go alone. Talk. Embrace what you are feeling. Express your emotions because then they start making some sense. Be gentle on yourself. It's fine to feel amazing at the start of the day and be absolutely devastated by nightfall. It's cool if you don't do anything. Ir's perfectly okay to discard your personal or social obligations. None of that matters if your mental health isn't fine. Prioritize your own well-being first. Do whatever helps you deal with it. And just to reiterate, hit me up if you want a sympathetic ear, a human pillow to scream into, or just someone to virtually hug you and say "there, there!"

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Do you think that China is hiding the actual facts and figures of casualties and those infected related to the COVID-19?
Answer: Yes. The Chinese Communist Party is notorious for its secrecy. And they would never allow anything that puts them in a negative light to be made public. There are multiple reasons to believe that China is deliberately underreporting the #s, especially the casualties in the wake of the COVID19 pandemic. #1: The disappearance of 15 million mobile subscribers. #2: Cemeteries working overtime China’s culture of lies has helped spread coronavirus The article is from Feb 8. At that time, there were just over 600 deaths in China. But the ground reality is otherwise. How many people in China have fallen victim to the coronavirus to date? One hint comes from how busy Wuhan’s 14 crematoriums have suddenly become. One crematorium manager told a Hong Kong reporter that, in normal times, his 24 ovens were lit five days a week for four hours at a time. Now, he said, they have so many corpses to deal with that all the ovens are going around the clock. This suggests the body count must be in the thousands. 14 crematoriums burning bodies 24x7. Assuming 100 per day per crematorium, we are talking about 1400 deaths per day during the early stages of the epidemic. Add to it the fact that China deployed 40 mobile crematoriums, so we could be talking about 3000–4000 bodies being burned every day. And then the urns — Report of Urns in Wuhan Raises Questions About COVID-19 Death Toll Outside one funeral home, trucks shipped in about 2,500 urns on both Wednesday and Thursday, according to Chinese media outlet Caixin. Another picture published by Caixin showed 3,500 urns stacked on the ground inside. It’s unclear how many of the urns had been filled. #3: Historical precedence from 2002–04 Chinese admit to SARS mistakes In a rare admission of serious mistakes, the Chinese government fired the minister of health and the mayor of Beijing yesterday for their early mishandling of the respiratory disease known as SARS, canceled a national weeklong holiday and reported almost 10 times as many SARS cases in Beijing, with hundreds more likely to come. So, yeah! FUCK THE CCP!

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What expression do you hate?
Answer: “starting a family” As someone who has been married for almost 5 years, this is the most irritating question I am asked, the assumption being that starting a family is the same as having kids, which is offensive, to say the least. My wife and I have been together for 13 years. But because we have chosen to not have kids, does that invalidate all those years? I believe we have evolved past that point where family referred to a man and a woman rearing kids. In the broader sense of the word, “family” described the people you care about and love and vice-versa. These are the ones you choose to spend time with. The ones you can bank on to provide emotional support during times of need. And that could be anything. A couple is a family. A gay couple is a family. A man and his dog are a family. Two friends living together are family. 5 men, a duck, a bear, and a lizard, raising an adoptive horse daughter are a family.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Will foreign businesses start to invest more in India post-Covid-19?
Answer: Maybe, maybe not. But if we do not act soon, the opportunity will already be gone. And the warning signs are already here — Indian economy in danger of being left behind in post-COVID world, warn experts. The exodus of companies shifting their manufacturing bases from China should have been the perfect opportunity for India to capitalize on. After all, both economies offer similar advantages in terms of labor costs, economies of scale, low cost of production, and skilled labor. However, “According to a recent study by Nomura, out of 56 companies shifting base from China, a mere three companies preferred India, while 26 decided to relocate to Vietnam. Taiwan was chosen by 11 firms and Thailand by 8 companies.” That is a dismal success ratio. And the culprit is the snail’s pace at which we function. The Indian government is mulling a strong boost to Make in India post the COVID-19 lockdown — Govt’s Covid-19 Revival Plan Includes Major Focus On Make In India. There is literally no reason to wait that long. In fact, the lockdown should have given enough time for the Ministry of Commerce to have a special committee come up with an actionable plan to leverage the opportunities in the market. On the other hand, Vietnam has already done so couple of weeks back — Vietnam Issues Incentives to Counter Impact of COVID-19 Impact. Vietnam had also emerged as the top beneficiary of the US-China trade war, another opportunity India was unable to capitalize on — Vietnam Is Becoming The Big Winner In The China Trade Wars. All this while, the Indian government’s push for single-brand FDI, the lucrative corporate tax reduction in the last year, and improvements in the Ease of Doing Business, have not yielded results anywhere as commensurate as expected. But all hope is not lost — 1,000 foreign firms mull production in India, 300 actively pursue plan as 'Exit China' mantra grows And this is what scares me the most. Indian bureaucracy and red-tape are infamous for still being hungover from the License Raj. I hope that this changes. That the Ministry of Commerce takes cognizance of how incredibly rare this opportunity is. That the global sentiment about India and Make in India is strong. That we have never been better poised in terms of infrastructure and our human capital to become the next economic powerhouse. I hope.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: How should we plan for our MBA now, with Covid19 causing a terrible economic impact?
Answer: I think Rohit has absolutely nailed it in his answer. What you are seeing now as in the market is pure panic. I mean, companies are laying off employees after just one month of muted or no operations? It seems like a knee-jerk reaction to me. However, the current pandemic will also have some long-lasting effects on all sectors, and consequently on the job market as well. The 2009 crisis was catastrophic for the graduating classes. And the 2020 situation will likely be equally bad — Poets&Quants | This Year’s MBA Job Market: How Bad Will It Get? At the top ten business schools, MBA employment rates at graduation dropped an average 21% from 2007. At the next 15 highly ranked schools, the drop was even steeper: 23%. At Harvard Business School in 2009, nearly one in four grads failed to have a job at graduation, as the employment rate fell to 76.8% from 94.3% two years earlier. At Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management, the employment rate for MBA grads slumped to 68.1% from 91.9%, a 25.6% decline in jobs. However, the hardest hit will be the people graduating right now, or next year. By 2022, we would already have weathered the worst of this storm. I will even venture as much to say that 2022 might be a better-than-average year for job prospects. Once this economic downturn fizzles out, a lot of weak companies would have closed shop. Most of the remaining ones would be running on minimal human power possible. But like after every trough, there is a crest, so will the market rebound once this is over. A lot of new startup ideas will germinate. Mature firms will look to pursue growth once more instead of focusing on minimizing their risk exposure. All in all, if this pandemic is truly contained by the end of 2020, we might be looking at a strong rebound which will benefit the 2022/23 classes the most. Anyway, it might not be the best time to be in the job market. Growth will be muted, both in terms of your profile and the money. There will be a constant risk of lay-offs if you are in a cash-heavy organization in an industry severely impacted by the lockdown. So, it might be prudent to take this opportunity to go back to college and acquire some new skills. A lot of colleges have waived off GMAT and GRE requirements considering the situation, so you can take a shot — Some graduate schools are waiving GRE test requirements because of COVID-19. After all, if you had planned to play outside and it started raining, do you still persist or go back and study while it pours?

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: After Covid19, how long will it take for the stock market to return to January 2020 levels?
Answer: At the very least a year, assuming the world is able to vanquish this virus in the next 3–4 months. In the worst case, more than double that. During the 2008–09 financial meltdown, global markets crashed by more than 50%. NASDAQ peaked at about 2800 in Nov 2007. On 27 Feb, 2009, it was lingering below 1400. It took another 2 years (Feb 2011) for it to regain the 2800 mark. The Indian SENSEX had a similar trajectory. The peak of about 20,200 in end-Dec 2007, followed by a trough of 8700 in Jan-end 2009. Although it was able to recoup the losses and breached the 20,000 mark again in Oct 2010. The ongoing crisis, even after it is quelled, may have a lingering impact on the overall global economy, with trade restrictions and subdued travel impacting export-oriented (China, India) and tourism-heavy (Thailand, Italy, larger Europe) economies. Also, the overall consumer sentiment might just have been changed for the long-term with people preferring to save instead of spend, in fear of another looming disaster like this. This would again impact consumer-oriented economies like the USA. Also, if the pandemic is prolonged, there will be bankruptcies and massive layoffs, coupled with hoarding and price-gouging, with the potential to plunge global economies into stagflation, which is a really bad scenario. The cost of dealing with the aftermath of the epidemic coupled with lower business and personal incomes will put a dent into the fiscal deficit of large countries, making the road to recovery even harder.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Will creating a live tracker (like Google Maps) with real-time details of coronavirus-affected people help control the spread? If yes, why is it not initiated yet?
Answer: For the following reasons: However, if you keep those apprehensions aside, there are still practical issues. The only proper use-case for cellphone tracking is to assess who all came in contact with an affected person prior to their testing positive. And a lot of countries are doing it — 19 countries track mobile location to fight COVID-19 Europe’s telecom companies are sharing location data with health authorities in Italy, Germany and Austria, according to Reuters, to check whether people are remaining at home. The data is aggregated and anonymous, mapping concentrations rather than individuals to respect Europe’s privacy laws. In South Korea, the government created a map of cellphone data provided by telecom and credit card companies. The map was made public so everyone could track whether they’d been exposed, according to The Verge. According to reports, Iran used the COVID-19 epidemic to gather private data from its citizens “to boost Tehran’s surveillance capabilities,” reports Vice. The country sent a link to download the AC19 app with government endorsement, touting it as a way to determine whether users have the virus, but usage required sending back location data. In Taiwan, a mobile phone-based geo-fence uses location-tracking to ensure people who are quarantined stay in their homes, reports the New York Times. If the patient leaves their home address or turns off their smartphone, the police will visit within 15 minutes.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: How viable is the idea of having "covid positive only allowed" restaurants, flights, movie halls, and pretty much any of the services? How will it be received?
Answer: That would be a very stupid idea. COVID is not a death sentence. If you contract it, there are high chances that you will recover in a couple of weeks if you do not have any existing conditions that can get complicated by the new viral infection. All you need to do is to go to a doctor, isolate yourself to protect others, take rest, and be patient. In 2–3 weeks, you should be almost fine and dandy. You SHOULD NOT be working or going out. COVID-only halls or restaurants would not be feasible. It takes far longer to open a new restaurant or convert one to this specific purpose. And even if you are able to, then what? Do you hire cooks who are COVID positive? Waiters? Movie hall staff? What happens when in 2 weeks they recover? Are you going to find new workers? How are you going to ensure that ALL of these people will follow proper precautions when they are out in public? Will you request a COVID-only Uber? Should companies change their overall operating strategy because a bunch of nincompoops can’t stay at home for a couple of weeks? Let’s not even talk about airlines. Are you going to ensure that all airport ground and air staff at both the source and destination are COVID positive? Would you trust an unwell pilot to take you through the air at thousand miles per hour in a pressurized metal container? People need to grow the fuck up. Make sacrifices for others. Behave like a community. Put the greater good over one’s own petty ideas of “freedom”. The world does not work in isolation. And it is high time that all seven billion people acknowledge that they “share” this planet and learn of their responsibilities alongside their rights.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why do Tesla’s Elon Musk calls Covid-19 lockdown restrictions fascist?
Answer: I just finished the book, “Winners Take All: The Elite Charade of Changing the World” by Anand Giridhardas. The main crux of it is that everything the rich and powerful do, even something as laudable as charity, is aligned with their core interests. Companies only want to change the world, if there is something in it for them. Alibaba only wants “to make it easy to do business anywhere” so that they can sell to every single of the 7 billion-plus people. Google wants “to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful” so that they can sell ads and make money. Coke wants to “refresh the world” so they can sell as much of sugary corn syrup drinks as they can. Elon is no different. He just wants what is best for him and his business. Despite the COVID shutdown in China in Q1 2020, Tesla production did not suffer much — Tesla kept global sales and production up despite coronavirus-related shutdowns Tesla delivered 88,400 vehicles in the first quarter of 2020, according to the release. That’s down from its best sales quarter ever at the end of 2019, where Tesla delivered around 112,000 vehicles. But it’s not nearly as low as the 63,000 the company shipped one year ago in the first quarter of 2019, and it beats out most estimates from Wall Street analysts as well as those from some of Tesla’s biggest supporters. However Q2 won’t fare as good — Tesla Producing Only 50K Cars In Q2? This article is from a month ago and Tesla units were only expected to remain closed till May 4 initially. Then there is also the fact that he has a direct, vested interest in maintaining production levels and, consequently, the stock price of Tesla above a certain threshold — Tesla's Musk nears $750 million options payday ahead of results Monday’s rally put Tesla’s market capitalization at $145 billion. Importantly for Musk, its stock market value reached a six-month average of $96 billion. Hitting a six-month average of $100 billion would trigger the vesting of the first of 12 tranches of options granted to the billionaire to buy Tesla stock as part of his two-year-old pay package. Each tranche gives Musk the option to buy 1.69 million Tesla shares at $350.02 each. Taking Monday’s Tesla closing stock price of $798.75 as an example, Musk could sell those shares for a profit of $758 million.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: How probable is it that the COVID-19 infection curve would have flattened by the end of the approximately six-week lockdown ending on 3 May?
Answer: Highly probable. The curve has already started to flatten in a few states, notably Kerala, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana, Andhra. The North-eastern states have very few cases, with Assam being the only outlier.[1] Odisha and Uttarakhand too are flattening. Karnataka isn’t really flattening but considering the size of the state, they have very few cases and are witnessing 10–15 new cases every day. The states/UTs facing the brunt of the problem are Maharashtra, Gujarat, Delhi NCR, Madhya Pradesh.[2] The 3-week lockdown is finally yielding results, and I am hopeful that the situation by 3rd of May will be far better. Do not expect the lockdown to be lifted across the country on 4th May though. Some of the hotspots like Delhi and Mumbai will remain sealed. However, the majority of the country might be able to resume work in some capacity.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Is the coronavirus that we are having right now among the worst in human history?
Answer: Not by a long shot. Not till now, and hopefully never. The ongoing Coronavirus/COVID-19 outbreak is deadly, no doubt. But the worst part about it is the nature of its virality — it is spreading at an unprecedented rate, with the number of confirmed cases doubling every 3 days or so.[1] In absolute terms, the stats currently are as follows[2] There are speculations that if a treatment is not developed soon, or if the spread of the disease is not curtailed by governments and the public, eventually ~50% of the world might get affected. The current stated mortality rate of 3%+ seems an exaggeration since a lot of people who contracted the virus (mild infection) likely didn’t get tested and got well, overstating the more serious cases.[3] Assuming a 1% mortality rate, the worst-case scenario would imply about 3.6 bn infected, and 36 million dead. This would be extremely tragic, but would still not compare with the Spanish Flu of 1918. [4] The Spanish Flu infected a quarter of the global population of about 2 billion at that time. Total infected were in about 500 million of which estimated casualties were about 50 million, implying that 2.5% of the global population perished because of it. But we need to remember that a century ago, we didn’t have the scientific temper and the medical advancements we have now. In fact, the world at that time did not even know that the flu was caused by a virus, and in fact, believed it was a bacterial infection. [5] The Spanish flu is frightening because it demonstrates that in a reasonably modern society, a pandemic killing tens of millions of people is very plausible. But that “reasonably modern” society was still much more primitive when it came to medicine and public health than the world of today. Here are a few facts about public health in the year 1918: So, the COVID-19 is not remotely the deadliest in human history, and it will never be. If only people follow the medical guidelines issued by health authorities worldwide, go to the doctor at the slightest sign of infection, duly self-quarantine themselves, and just be cautious for the next month or two, we have the infrastructure and the facilities required to treat the infected and the rate of spread would drastically decline.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Will the world still be a same place after coronavirus, or it will change?
Answer: I hope it changes. The COVID19 pandemic should be treated as a warning. Viruses and infectious diseases have been a part and parcel of human history from its inception. However, this truly might be the biggest, most devastating one in modern history. The Spanish Flu outbreak happened over a century ago. Since then, the world has changed so much that it is unrecognizable. We have made advancements in science and technology by leaps and bounds. The first commercial flight took place in 1914, just a few years before the Spanish Flu and today more than 4 billion people fly every year. Globalization. The advent of the internet. The population today is more than 4x what it was a century back. And everything is so interconnected that the entire world has been brought to halt because of one person eating a bat/pangolin. We truly are living in an era of unprecedented connectivity. The world has shrunk and the chances that another “butterfly effect” might just be the ruin of all of humanity have increased drastically. As such, the Novel Coronavirus is indeed “Novel”. We have not seen the likes of it in a long time, and absolutely not in the current setting. So the year 2020 should ideally work as a warning/template/learning opportunity for all federal governments and the global humanity for years to come. There are more. And more will spring up as this year passes (GOD! Let it pass faster.)

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: How long does it take to get over severe heartbreak?
Answer: You do not get over a heartbreak, you get through it. There’s a beautiful couplet by Jigar Moradabadi. ये इश्क़ नहीं आसाँ इतना ही समझ लीजे इक आग का दरिया है और डूब के जाना है which roughly translates to Heed - this journey of love isn’t easy, A river of fire; to be crossed submerged. To be honest, you never “completely” get over someone. Just like the half-life decay of radioactive elements, you never truly reach a state where the heartbreak ceases to exist. But the good news is that it gets easier. With every single passing day. With every word of validation from friends and family. With every new person you meet who rekindles the hope of finding love again. With every moment of self-reflection and self-acceptance. I ask that you read this Twitter thread - one of my favorites ever since I stumbled across it fortuitously at my lowest last year. Your healing journey is your own. No one can tell you how to get over a heartbreak. That is something you have to figure out on your own. I won’t tell you what to do. Just what I did. And hope that it helps you figure out your own path. The first thing I did was get ride of the self-blame. For a long time, I was angry at myself - for the mistakes I had made (inadverently), I chided myself - “should have done better”. Until I realized that such thoughts do not help. No one is perfect; people make mistakes. And sometimes they get second chances, but other times they don’t. Next I let of the anger and the resentment. I offered her the same courtesy I did to myself. We both were human, we both made mistakes. Finally, acceptance. I realized that life is complicated and unpredictable. And often, despite your best efforts, it doesn’t go the way you had planned because there are a lot of externalities at play. You can’t fight an earthquake, you can’t outrun a storm. All you can do is find shelter till it passes away. And then salvage what you can from the ruins and rebuild. Think of healing as an actual, physical journey. You’ve been thrown into the wilderness with no preparation. The first few days are excruciating. You feel lost, desolate, overpowered by despair. But the only way is through. All you can do is start walking. Your feet blister, your legs hurt. The thickets cut you, the sun scorches your skin. And every single day, you have to fight the urge to give up. But you need to persist. Your stamina increases. You figure out the navigation. You unlock the balance between continuing and resting. The blisters heal. The scars start to fade. One day you realize you are at the prescipice of the forest and you finally step out. While the tumultous journey is over, it stays with you. You get the occasional nightmare. But eventually you accept and embrace the experience. Another facet of life. The scars now part of your identity.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What can you do during 14 days of the Coronavirus quarantine period?
Answer: Amidst the global frenzy in the wake of the COVID-19 outbreak, a lot of people will find themselves socially isolated and quarantined, mostly involuntarily. For people who are accustomed to a hectic life, this might be daunting, especially confined within the four walls of their homes, with no idea what to do. However, such “downtime” can be made productive and leisurely. You could always revisit a childhood hobby, something you abandoned before duties and responsibilities occupied every waking moment of every day. Or you could pick up a new one, something you have always wanted to learn but could never find the time to. There are instructional DIY videos and detailed lessons for beginners on Youtube on almost every topic conceivable. If you want to relax, there’s an inconceivable amount of literature and art online to consume. Download a new ebook to read. Or visit Project Gutenberg to get your hands on thousands of “classic” works that are in the public domain. Hit up your Netflix or Hulu account and watch some good movies. I am going to be exploring more of world cinema and watching movies and shows in languages other than Hindi or English. I just saw Parasite a month ago and I am currently binge-watching Money Heist. You could watch the French classic Amelie, or the painfully funny German tragicomedy A Coffee in Berlin. Non-Indians could explore wonderful Bollywood movies like Udaan, 3 Idiots, Andhadhun, The Lunchbox, Stree, etc. Animation fans, especially from the Western nations could step out of their comfort zones of Disney, Pixar, and Dreamworks and explore the mesmerizing creation of Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli — Spirited Away, My Neighbor Totoro, The Red Turtle, Kiki’s Delivery Service. You could take this time to think of something new — academicians could publish a paper, techies could develop a new app or a new website, entrepreneurs could just seed the next unicorn. Comic enthusiasts could purchase a DC/Marvel/Comxiology subscription and catch up on the last few years of stories they have missed. The musical souls could finally pen and record a song, who knows there’s the next Ed Sheeran or Taylor Swift, hiding somewhere in their apartment, bogged down by their daily obligations to dedicate time to their art. If you have a great voice and in-depth knowledge about any topic, start a new podcast. It requires minimal set-up and could very well become a great secondary source of income. Working professionals can learn a new subject or complete an online course or certification to boost their profile, to diversify their skill set, or just for the sake of learning something new. I have shared some good resources on my UoQ (University of Quora) space. If you have always wanted to get in shape, you can start forming the habit now — you don’t even need equipment to start training your body — The 7 Best at Home Workouts (No-Equipment Required). People who stay alone could learn how to cook, a skill that is absolutely essential yet forgotten in a world where everything from groceries to gourmet meals is just at the tap of a few buttons. You’d not only be eating healthier, but you will also save a lot of money (once this outbreak dies off, and God! let that be quick). At the same time, cooking, at least in my personal opinion is a great destresser. This list is by no means comprehensive, but you get the idea. Quarantine doesn’t have to be dull and unrewarding. With some planning and effort, it could be a great time to catch up on life or plan what lies ahead.

Question: Do you think India's Corona curve would have flattened or went on a decline if you remove the cases due to Tablighi Jamat?
Answer: The curve wouldn’t have flattened, but it surely wouldn’t be rising exponentially if the Tablighi Jamaat incident had not happened. I have taken the day-wise Coronavirus data from Wiki[1] and the number of cases directly attributed to the Tablighi Jamaat from various news sources. These numbers might not be accurate to the tee, but give us enough required information. You can see that the daily number of new cases were hovering in the 100s before Mar 31st. But the daily number shot up to 400+ from Mar 31st as the various governments started contact tracing of the attendees. Of the total 4200+ cases in India, one-third (1445) can be traced back to the congregation. This one event has reduced the time for total cases to double by over 40%, from 7.4 days to 4.1 days.[7] The ministry’s updated data came a day after it said the rate of doubling of Covid-19 cases in India accelerated to 4.1 days from the estimated 7.4 days due to the Jamaat event in Nizamuddin West last month.

And we haven’t heard anything from them about the coronavirus epidemic, nor have we seen any actions from their side to utilize their wealth and influence to help India as a nation to combat it. We have had them host some of the most expensive and over-the-top weddings for their kids, where movie stars and music artists from all over the world came and performed, in a ludicrous display of debauchery. They are busy tweeting memes. Or just stuck in their narrow worldview, trying just to protect their businesses — Coronavirus impact: Mukesh Ambani pads up to protect half a million Reliance employees Or tweeting bullshit, feel-good, useless, gratitude statements.
